title: Workflow Automation Guide: Build and Test Your First Process
desc: Define a trigger, owner and exception path, calculate realistic time released, and test duplicate events before rolling out a small-business workflow.
text:
## What workflow automation actually does
Workflow automation runs a defined sequence when an event occurs. A request form can create an internal task; an approved task can update a record. The useful result is correct work reaching the correct owner with enough context. A green run indicator alone does not prove that the destination contains the right result.
Start with an internal, reversible workflow. Keep payment approval, unusual customer promises and irreversible actions with an authorized person until the relevant controls exist. This guide explains design and acceptance; it does not connect your accounts. Use the [business process guide](/journal/business-process-automation/) for the wider operating process.
## Write a one-page workflow contract
Record the source event, required fields, condition, action, destination, owner and completion evidence. For an inbound service request, require a stable request ID, supported service category and authorized contact route. Check whether that request already has a destination task. Create one internal review task, save its ID and assign the operations reviewer. Incomplete requests enter a named exception queue rather than generating a customer promise.
Distinguish the business event ID from the execution ID: two execution attempts may describe the same request. Retain both IDs, workflow version and final disposition. Confirm that required destination fields match the source before calling the task complete. Set a backup owner before the reviewer is absent.
## Calculate time released after exceptions
Fictional monthly pilot: 200 requests at four manual minutes each use 800 minutes. Of those, 180 follow the automated path and need one review minute each. Twenty exceptions still take four minutes each. Maintenance adds 60 minutes. New effort is 180 + 80 + 60 = 320 minutes. Capacity released is 480 minutes, or eight hours.
At an entered planning rate of $25 per hour, released capacity is valued at $200. Less an assumed $50 recurring tool cost leaves $150 of monthly planning benefit. A $300 setup cost has a simple two-month payback only if the assumptions remain true. Released capacity is not payroll savings unless spending actually falls. Do not count both its full labor value and new sales from the same hours without allocating those hours.
## Test the normal and failure paths
Submit one valid request and confirm exactly one correctly assigned task. Replay the same request twice and inspect the destination count. Remove a required field and verify that a person receives the exception. Simulate a timeout after the destination writes the task: reconcile the destination before retrying, because a timeout does not prove nothing happened.
Use an expired connection and verify that a named operator sees the failure. Pause intake, document the manual queue and rehearse a controlled restart. Retries can help temporary outages; they do not fix invalid permissions. Avoid logging credentials or unnecessary customer content in broadly shared logs.
## Pilot, inspect and expand
Compare unique source requests with completed destination records, unresolved exceptions and duplicates. Measure all operator minutes, including maintenance. Review the oldest unresolved item beside the completion percentage. If results are wrong, pause intake and preserve the event register before any replay.
For campaign work, use the [marketing pilot](/journal/marketing-automation-small-business/); for identity and field updates use [CRM record controls](/journal/crm-automation-guide/). Reserve actual maintenance time in the [weekly time-blocking worksheet](/tools/time-blocking-template/). A process that nobody has time to monitor is not ready for expansion.
## Frequently asked questions
Do I need AI? No. Known conditions often work with deterministic rules. If AI classifies text, define the uncertain-result path and the human reviewer.
Which tool is best? Test required connectors, permissions, run history, replay behavior and exportability against your actual workflow. This is not a vendor ranking or subscription certification.
When is the pilot ready? When the agreed source sample reconciles, exceptions have owners, duplicate tests pass and the manual fallback has been demonstrated.

title: Marketing Automation for Small Business: A Measurable Pilot
desc: Plan one marketing journey with eligibility, suppression and sales handoff rules, then measure an original contribution-based pilot example.
text:
## Choose one journey and one outcome
Marketing automation coordinates campaign actions using recorded audience events and conditions. Begin with one journey, such as a requested resource followed by an eligible consultation invitation. Define success as a useful customer action rather than more sends. A new contact record does not establish permission for every channel.
This page owns campaign design across stages. The [email automation guide](/journal/email-marketing-automation/) covers send-level timing; the [sales automation guide](/journal/sales-automation-guide/) covers an accepted handoff into a deal process. Keep those outcomes distinct when reporting results.
## Define entry, exit and handoff
At entry, retain the source event and the eligibility decision. Segment using stated relevant interests rather than inferred sensitive traits. Before each outward action, recheck suppression and whether the customer has already reached the goal. If a consultation is requested, create a task and require the named sales owner to accept it.
Exit on opt-out, goal completion, invalid destination or manual hold. Record the reason and cancel obsolete steps. Define re-entry explicitly: a repeat page visit should not restart the same journey without a deliberate rule. An imported list must not overwrite a prior opt-out. Choose an authoritative suppression decision across the connected systems.
## Separate observed activity from incremental value
Original fictional experiment: randomly split 1,000 eligible contacts into 500 pilot and 500 holdout contacts. In the same review window, the pilot records 30 qualifying orders and the holdout records 20. Rates are 6% and 4%; the observed difference is two percentage points. With equal groups, the raw incremental-order estimate is ten.
At an assumed $40 contribution per qualifying order after the declared variable costs, estimated incremental contribution is $400. Subtract $250 of incremental campaign and tool costs for a $150 pilot contribution estimate. Do not subtract costs already included in the $40 twice.
This small example does not establish a reliable causal effect. Inspect assignment, uncertainty, cancellations, cross-group exposure and timing. Without a valid comparison, describe attributed orders rather than calling every order incremental. Use the [campaign budget worksheet](/tools/marketing-campaign-budget-planner/) to keep costs explicit.
## Prepare a compact campaign brief
Write the audience definition, event source, eligibility owner, customer promise and destination. Assign a reviewer for copy and accessibility. State the timezone, delay, stop conditions and pause procedure. Define the qualifying outcome, cohort, measurement window and cost boundary before viewing results.
Agree the handoff fields with sales before enabling intake. Passing an unqualified list is not an accepted lead. Connect the brief to the [one-page marketing plan](/journal/one-page-marketing-plan-example/) so that the automation serves an objective instead of becoming the objective.
## Run a controlled trial
Test an eligible contact, a suppressed contact, a duplicate event and a contact who reaches the goal during the delay. Verify that pausing prevents new outward actions and that the intended destination exists. Use harmless records rather than contacting customers as a test without authorization.
Inspect unexpected re-entry, unresolved exceptions and actual customer outcomes before increasing volume. Assign time for replies and manual review. Keep the [workflow acceptance checklist](/journal/workflow-automation-guide/) and [CRM authority register](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) beside the campaign brief; a campaign can fail because its data is wrong even when each message step runs.
## Frequently asked questions
Should I automate all channels? Start with one journey and one channel that the team can support and measure. Add complexity only after the first path works.
Are opens enough? They describe a limited engagement signal. Use a qualifying action, declared denominator and clear cost boundary for the business decision.
Does this send campaigns? No. These guides and manual worksheets plan the work; they do not provide live email sending, a CRM connection or automatic eligibility verification.

title: Business Process Automation: Ownership, Cost and Controls
desc: Map an end-to-end process, assign approval and exception owners, and evaluate a purchase-request automation with original cost and sensitivity examples.
text:
## Start with the operating outcome
Business process automation addresses an outcome across tasks and owners. A notification may automate one task; the complete process also needs intake, approvals, execution, reconciliation and closure. Remove unnecessary steps before speeding them up. Faster unnecessary work still wastes effort.
This page owns end-to-end design and prioritization. Use the [workflow guide](/journal/workflow-automation-guide/) for one event-triggered build and [CRM guide](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) for record ownership. A process can combine connected software and human decisions without being fully automatic.
## Map a purchase request to closure
The requester records purpose, quantity, unit and a stable request ID. The budget owner checks need and funding, returning incomplete requests. An authorized approver records the decision and request version. Purchasing creates an order only after required approval. Receiving matches accepted units to that order. Finance reviews the invoice and differences before payment. The process owner closes remaining exceptions.
Automation can route work and retain evidence; it cannot invent approval authority. A changed quantity, supplier or price may require renewed review. Define which changes invalidate approval. Use the [purchase requisition worksheet](/tools/purchase-requisition-template/) for manual preparation, while retaining the actual authority policy separately.
## Compare effort including rework
Fictional monthly baseline: 120 requests at eight minutes use 960 minutes. Proposed normal handling takes three minutes per request, or 360 minutes. Twelve exceptions add ten minutes each beyond normal handling, or 120 minutes. Maintenance takes another 120 minutes. Proposed effort is 600 minutes, releasing 360 minutes or six hours.
At an assumed $30 per hour, capacity value is $180. Less $90 recurring automation cost leaves $90 monthly planning benefit. A $540 setup cost has simple payback of six months under these assumptions. Capacity value is not a verified reduction in payroll or proof that the process will remain stable.
If exceptions rise to 30 requests, effort becomes 360 + 300 + 120 = 780 minutes. Only three hours are released, valued at $90. After the $90 recurring cost there is no recurring planning benefit and no finite simple payback. Exception volume can reverse the decision even when the normal path remains fast.
## Select a bounded first candidate
Prefer stable inputs, an observable volume, reversible actions and a named process owner. Check whether the actual systems expose the necessary fields and permissions. Inspect conflicting definitions before connecting systems: two departments using different customer IDs have an ownership issue, not simply a missing connector.
A score can organize discussion but is not a guarantee. Record the evidence for each rating, including who will maintain rules, investigate failures and review aging exceptions. Keep an affordable manual fallback for the pilot. Confirm the monitoring workload fits the team's available time.
## Accept business results rather than run status
Test a normal request, missing unit, changed request after approval, absent approver, duplicate event and partial receipt. Every unfinished item needs an owner and next review date. Reconcile requested, approved, ordered and received quantities separately; none proves that the bank payment occurred.
Use the [purchase order tracking guide](/journal/purchase-order-tracker/) for quantity boundaries and the [operations dashboard example](/journal/operations-dashboard-example/) for due-cohort reporting. Keep an aging exception list beside completion counts. If a connection fails after a destination write, reconcile before replaying the request.
## Frequently asked questions
Is BPA the same as RPA? RPA is one implementation approach that can operate interfaces. Business process automation is the wider design, which may also use connectors, rules and manual approval.
Must every system be replaced? No. Confirm one working path and its data contract before expanding.
What stops a rollout? Unowned exceptions, duplicate external actions, missing approval evidence or an unreconciled destination justify pausing and repairing the process.

title: Customer-Service Automation: Escalation and Real Resolution
desc: Design support routing and human handoff, measure reopened tickets with clear denominators, and calculate a bounded customer-service capacity example.
text:
## Automate the repeatable part of support
Customer-service automation can acknowledge a request, collect necessary context, route a ticket or offer an approved answer. A fast acknowledgment is not a solved problem. Start with a narrow request type whose answer can be checked, such as locating a current setup guide. Keep unusual complaints, refunds and access changes with an authorized owner.
Rules-based routing does not need generative AI. If a model suggests answers, define the approved knowledge source, uncertainty path and reviewer. This guide designs an operating process; it does not deploy a chatbot or access customer records.
## Write the human handoff first
For a recognized setup question, offer the relevant current help section and a clear route to a person. Missing information should trigger a request for the minimum necessary reference. Unknown issues enter a named queue with original context. A refund request is routed for approval rather than automatically approved. Repeat contact should bring the earlier issue into view.
Do not ask for passwords or payment secrets in tickets. Define access to attachments and appropriate retention for the actual records. The [CRM guide](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) explains record identity; the [workflow guide](/journal/workflow-automation-guide/) explains duplicate and retry controls. A reliable route matters more than an impressive-looking bot response.
## Use a fixed resolution cohort
Original fictional cohort: 100 tickets enter in one week. Forty are marked resolved without an agent. During the stated follow-up window, eight reopen for the same issue. Thirty-two remain resolved without an agent in that window, giving an adjusted automated-resolution share of 32%. The reopen share among the 40 auto-resolved tickets is 20%. Those are different denominators.
State the follow-up window because a later reopening may revise the result. A ticket disappearing from an active queue is not sufficient evidence of resolution. Preserve its cohort when it changes status; otherwise repeated closures can inflate a success measure.
## Calculate net support effort
Assume the 100 tickets would each otherwise take ten agent minutes, giving 1,000 baseline minutes. Sixty routed tickets plus eight reopened tickets require ten minutes each, or 680 minutes. Add 80 minutes of knowledge maintenance and review. Total effort is 760 minutes, releasing 240 minutes or four hours.
This simplified example assumes ticket groups do not overlap and excludes initial setup. It does not prove payroll savings. Add actual investigation and maintenance costs when evaluating a real pilot. Do not count a reopened issue as both a new independent customer and a successful old resolution without explaining the measures.
## Carry useful context and test quality
A handoff should include the original request, verified reference, steps attempted, relevant article version and why automation stopped. Preserve customer words separately from generated summaries. Let an agent inspect and correct the underlying record. Avoid making the customer repeat troubleshooting because the issue moved queues.
Test a supported question, ambiguity, repeated request, another customer's order reference and a reopened issue. Confirm that no unauthorized information is revealed and that a manual queue works during a pause. Align expectations with actual staffed hours rather than promising an unstaffed response time.
Use the [operations dashboard guide](/journal/operations-dashboard-example/) to keep overdue promises visible. Inspect unresolved and reopened issues alongside speed and volume. A drop in tickets can mean customers abandoned a channel; silence is not confirmed satisfaction.
## Frequently asked questions
Is a chatbot necessary? No. Routing, acknowledgments and an accurate help library may be the better first step.
Can automation approve refunds? That depends on a real authorized policy and tested implementation. This guide grants no approval authority.
Which metric comes first? Start with a fixed cohort, an explicit resolution outcome and a human escalation measure. Speed is useful alongside quality, not as a substitute.

title: Email Marketing Automation: Triggers, Stops and Metrics
desc: Design a controlled email sequence with send-time suppression, goal exits and unique-recipient reporting. Includes an original delivery reconciliation.
text:
## Define the event before the sequence
Email marketing automation sends a prepared message when a recorded event and its eligibility conditions match. Examples include a requested resource or an eligible follow-up. The system needs reliable recipient identity, relevant eligibility and stop rules. A service question does not automatically request a promotional series.
This page owns message timing and sequence checks. Use the [marketing pilot guide](/journal/marketing-automation-small-business/) for campaign strategy and [CRM record controls](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) to keep identity and suppression decisions consistent. This page does not enroll or contact anyone.
## Plan controlled steps and exits
At entry, retain the request event and validate the recipient and resource. For resource delivery, guard against duplicate events and verify the destination. A hypothetical follow-up two days later must recheck suppression and goal status. A consultation request can trigger an accepted sales handoff; an opt-out, completed goal or manual hold should stop obsolete promotional steps.
The two-day delay is a fictional design choice, not universal advice. Define the timezone and behavior during a pause. A person can opt out after enrollment but before a delayed send, so entry-only checks are insufficient. Confirm actual provider features and subscription limits in the account before relying on them.
## Reconcile people, attempts and deliveries
Fictional single-message cohort: 300 unique people enter. Before the scheduled send, 20 are suppressed and ten reach the goal. That leaves 270 unique send attempts. Six bounce and 264 are reported delivered. If 33 distinct delivered recipients click a qualifying link, the unique click share is 33 ÷ 264 = 12.5%.
A total of 42 clicks may include repeat clicks; it is not a 42-person numerator. Delivery is not proof that a person read the email or that it reached the inbox. Declare both the qualifying event and denominator before comparing reports.
Suppose twelve qualifying orders are attributed within the stated window at an entered contribution of $25 each. Attributed contribution is $300 before incremental costs not already included. Without a valid comparison group, those orders are not proven incremental orders. Keep campaign costs in the [budget worksheet](/tools/marketing-campaign-budget-planner/).
## Preflight the actual message
Confirm sender identity and a working reply route. Check recipient eligibility and current suppression. Test every link and the promised resource version. Preview narrow-screen rendering and useful plain text. Retain the required sender and opt-out information for the actual provider and applicable jurisdiction. Provider-specific unsubscribe instructions do not make all platforms identical.
Test a duplicate event, opt-out during a delay, purchase exit and paused queue. Use harmless authorized records. Avoid broad reenrollment of an old audience when editing a sequence. Inspect pending contacts and workflow version rather than assuming a new message definition affects every queued record in the intended way.
## Operate without losing message state
Retain enrollment, sequence version, intended message step, send attempt and final provider result. A retry refers to the same intended message event. After an uncertain timeout, inspect provider records before sending again, because the original request may have succeeded.
Review replies and failures beside clicks. Stop or revise messages that create confusion or complaints. Reserve review time in the [weekly worksheet](/tools/time-blocking-template/) and document who can pause the sequence. A technically successful send can still fail the customer promise.
## Frequently asked questions
Can a purchased list be used automatically? Do not assume a purchase establishes eligibility or meets provider requirements. Verify the actual source and applicable rules before any enrollment.
Does delivered mean opened? No. Keep attempted, delivered, unique engaged and qualifying outcomes separate.
Will this page send messages? No. It provides design guidance, not a sending service or automatic compliance check. Follow the actual provider's current documentation for account setup and applicable requirements.

title: Sales Automation Guide: Handoffs, Capacity and Pipeline
desc: Design accepted lead handoffs, calculate whole-lead capacity and separate weighted pipeline from actual cash before automating sales tasks.
text:
## Automate coordination before persuasion
Sales automation handles repeatable actions such as assigning a lead, creating a follow-up task or flagging a stalled proposal. Value depends on a real owner and next action. An automatic task does not prove customer contact; an automatic stage change does not prove a sale.
Keep negotiated terms, unusual prices and capacity promises with an authorized reviewer. A template reduces repeated preparation without removing the seller's responsibility. The [business proposal template](/tools/business-proposal-template/) prepares a bounded scope and itemized draft rather than sending or signing an agreement.
## Define an accepted handoff
An inquiry needs a stable ID and source. Qualification adds the relevant need, timing and contact eligibility. An accepted lead has a named owner who accepts the next action. A proposal requires reviewed scope, price and delivery assumptions. A won or lost outcome needs decision evidence and should stop obsolete follow-ups.
The [marketing guide](/journal/marketing-automation-small-business/) owns audience entry; the [CRM guide](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) owns record identity. This page owns lead-to-deal execution. One conversion should not be counted again merely because its record moved between systems. Retain an exception owner when automatic routing cannot decide.
## Check capacity before increasing lead flow
Original fictional week: 80 inquiries arrive; 50 meet the declared acceptance rule. A salesperson has 15 hours, or 900 minutes, for the work. Each accepted lead needs an initial twelve minutes and two six-minute follow-ups, totaling 24 minutes. Fifty leads require 1,200 minutes, leaving a 300-minute gap.
Under those assumptions, whole-lead capacity is floor(900 ÷ 24) = 37, with twelve minutes remaining. The other thirteen leads need another owner or an honest queue. Automation that saves three administrative minutes per lead reduces effort to 21 minutes and raises whole-lead capacity to 42, still below fifty.
Do not remove conversation and review time merely because administration becomes faster. Measure actual saved effort and keep the [capacity planning example](/journal/agency-capacity-planning-example/) beside the forecast. A routing rule cannot create additional delivery hours.
## Keep pipeline separate from cash
Five $2,000 proposals with an explicitly assumed 40% win probability give $10,000 nominal pipeline and $4,000 weighted pipeline. Neither is an invoice, receipt or money available to spend. If all five win together, delivery needs capacity for five jobs, not two expected jobs.
A weighted scenario and full-win stress test answer different questions. Record probability assumptions; do not present them as observed certainty. Separate sale date, invoice date and collection date. Model receipts with the [cash flow forecast](/journal/cash-flow-forecast-template-example/) instead of inserting weighted pipeline into opening bank cash.
## Test ownership and stop rules
Submit one lead, then replay its event: expect one accepted record and one next-action task. Route an event outside staffed hours and preserve the actual next staffed review window. Assign an absent owner and verify the backup process. Mark a deal lost and confirm obsolete follow-ups stop. Change proposal scope and require renewed review before sending.
Simulate a connector failure and reconcile the destination before retrying. Review accepted leads lacking next actions, unowned items and overdue tasks. Task completion is not the same as customer outcome. Keep attempts, replies, qualified opportunities and signed work separate in reporting.
## Frequently asked questions
Is a CRM enough? A CRM stores records; routing and automation depend on actual features and implementation. This guide does not certify subscriptions or connectors.
Should every lead receive one sequence? Match the next action to source, need, eligibility and stage. Stop when circumstances change.
Does weighted pipeline predict receipts? It is an assumption-based planning view. Collection timing needs separate evidence. Do not fund expenses from an expected-value number that has not been collected.

title: CRM Automation Guide: Clean Records, Rules and Exceptions
desc: Assign field authority, reconcile contact imports and test safe record transitions before using CRM automation across sales and service.
text:
## Make the record dependable first
CRM automation applies rules to relationship records: assign an owner, create a task or change a stage after a qualifying event. It cannot fix unclear ownership on its own. Define what one person, company, inquiry and deal mean in the actual system. These are separate entities with separate IDs.
This page owns record quality and transitions. The [sales guide](/journal/sales-automation-guide/) owns selling actions and [service guide](/journal/customer-service-automation/) owns ticket resolution. A single owner can start with the [solopreneur CRM routine](/journal/crm-for-solopreneurs/) before adding connections.
## Assign authority to fields
The CRM identity register owns the contact ID; an import row number should not replace it. A verified change process owns email updates. An authoritative suppression record owns marketing opt-outs. The sales owner and supporting evidence own deal stages; the support issue owner owns resolution status. Retain source event, timestamp and version for changes.
An email address can assist matching but is not a universal identity key. Shared addresses and changed addresses need review. An overly strict duplicate rule can merge different people; no rule can create several records for one person. Preserve an audit trail for an approved merge and keep its decision separate from ordinary updates.
## Reconcile every import disposition
Fictional import: 100 source rows contain 70 confirmed existing-contact updates, twenty new contacts, six duplicate source events and four ambiguous identities. All 100 rows are accounted for. Ninety rows apply as updates or creates; six are skipped with event references; four remain with a named reviewer.
If the CRM starts with 500 contacts, expected count is 520 before separate merges or deletions, not 590. Updates change existing records rather than increasing count. The four unresolved identities remain visible; silently forcing them into new contacts would make the reconciliation look complete while damaging the data.
Replaying the same import should leave count at 520 and not reissue follow-up tasks. Count agreement alone is insufficient: inspect field values and a destination-ID sample. Record source events and outcomes so a retry can find the original decision.
## Prevent update loops and stale writes
A field update may trigger another rule that changes the first field again. Limit transitions to a declared starting state, retain the causing event and avoid an unguarded trigger on every update. Where supported, version checks can reject an older write rather than overwriting a newer decision. Verify actual product behavior; this guide cannot guarantee a connector implements those controls.
Treat bulk merges and deletions separately from routine edits. Keep an authorized export and rehearse restoration with harmless data before depending on it. An export is not a working restore until the destination can recreate the necessary relationships. Limit access to sensitive fields and avoid copying unnecessary personal details into logs.
## Run a narrow acceptance pack
Test a valid new person, known person with one changed field, duplicate event, shared address, older timestamp, suppressed contact reimport and competing field update from two systems. Preserve unrelated fields on partial updates. Hold contradictory identity for review. Retain suppression when an old audience export is imported.
Compare both source register and destination, not only run status. Give each unresolved decision an owner and approval route. Use the [workflow guide](/journal/workflow-automation-guide/) for event replay and failure handling. Do not expand the integration while ownership conflicts remain unexplained.
## Frequently asked questions
Is automation the same as synchronization? Synchronization copies agreed fields between systems; automation uses events and rules to act. Either can exist separately.
Should deduplication use email alone? Use a documented identity policy suitable for the records and review ambiguous matches.
Do NexalyPlanner offline tools sync to a CRM? Do not infer that from these guides. Read the exact product documentation. This page provides no connector, hosted account or automatic synchronization.

title: How to Start a Business: Evidence Gates and a Launch Plan
desc: Build a US-focused launch plan around customer evidence, delivery capacity, cash timing and official requirements before increasing commitments.
text:
## Use evidence gates rather than a shopping list
Starting a business combines operating decisions with requirements that depend on activity and location. Use evidence gates: confirm the customer problem, test an offer, check capacity and cash, verify applicable requirements and run a controlled launch. This hub does not choose a legal structure or determine tax obligations.
Use the [business planning hub](/journal/business-plan-guide/) for the full plan and [industry examples](/journal/business-plan-examples/) for worked operating models. This page owns launch sequencing rather than repeating every industry plan or inventing a directory of untested ideas.
## Gate 1: test a specific offer
Describe one customer, one problem, one deliverable and the next action. Keep the source and date of customer evidence. A positive comment differs from a qualified request, which differs from a paid order. Avoid committing to substantial inventory or a lease solely because an untested forecast looks attractive.
Compare operating demands in the [business idea worksheet](/tools/business-idea-comparison/). Turn a particular client scope into a [proposal draft](/tools/business-proposal-template/). The proposal supports a customer decision; the business plan explains how the wider operation works. Neither document alone proves demand or acceptance.
## Gate 2: reconcile price, capacity and cash
Fictional service launch: eight jobs sell for $500 each, with $150 variable cost per job. Contribution is $350 per job. Fixed operating costs of $1,400 require four whole jobs to cover that cost boundary. At eight jobs, revenue is $4,000, variable cost $1,200 and operating surplus $1,400 before tax, owner compensation or other stated omissions.
Each job needs six delivery hours, so eight require 48 hours. A forty-hour delivery window supports only six whole jobs. A financially attractive sales forecast can still exceed available capacity. Decide how to change delivery dates, scope or staffing before promising all eight jobs.
Now separate cash timing. Opening cash $3,000 minus setup outlay $1,800, fixed outflow $1,400 and variable payments $1,200, plus only $2,000 collected revenue, leaves $600 closing cash. The other $2,000 remains uncollected in this simplified case. A $1,000 reserve is missed by $400. Use the [cash forecast guide](/journal/cash-flow-forecast-template-example/) before choosing a launch date.
## Gate 3: check actual requirements
The IRS starting-business checklist is explicitly not exhaustive and points to state requirements. Start with official sources for the real activity and location. Confirm applicable registrations, tax IDs, permits, employment obligations and records with the relevant authority or qualified adviser. Do not treat a generic checklist as evidence that every requirement is satisfied.
Maintain a register with activity, location, official authority, applicability decision, evidence date, responsible owner and confirmed deadline. Retain actual receipts or approvals where required. The [startup checklist](/tools/business-startup-checklist/) can organize tasks, but ticking a box does not replace official acceptance. Leave unresolved requirements visible rather than making a universal filing claim.
## Gate 4: pilot an operating workflow
Practice an inquiry, scope review, order, delivery record, invoice and collection entry using harmless data. Assign changes and complaints. Confirm the actual tools provide the promised functions before claiming automation or synchronization. Apply the [workflow guide](/journal/workflow-automation-guide/) only after the manual process works.
Choose a narrow route: [marketing intake](/journal/marketing-automation-small-business/), [email follow-up](/journal/email-marketing-automation/), [sales handoff](/journal/sales-automation-guide/), [CRM maintenance](/journal/crm-automation-guide/) or [support routing](/journal/customer-service-automation/). The [process guide](/journal/business-process-automation/) connects handoffs without making software selection the launch objective.
## Gate 5: review the first period
Compare completed work with promises, earned revenue with receipts and available hours with commitments. Record which assumptions failed and the evidence for change. Expand only when demand, delivery and cash support the same plan. Use a [weekly business review](/journal/business-planner-weekly-review/) rather than relying on the original forecast indefinitely.
## Frequently asked questions
Should I automate before finding customers? Build enough process for a bounded pilot without automating assumptions that remain untested.
Is profit enough? Capacity, startup spending and collection timing can still prevent delivery.
Does this establish legal readiness? No. Requirements depend on the activity and location; resolve relevant open items with official evidence.
